title: Shortest Stretch Worth at Least K
statement:
You get an integer array nums, which may contain negative numbers, and a positive integer k. Find the shortest non-empty contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k.

Return its length, or -1 if no subarray reaches k.

examples.why: [−2, 5] = 3 and [5] = 5 fall short. Only the whole array, 3 − 2 + 5 = 6, reaches 6.
[3, 4] = 7. A plain sliding window that grows from the left never sheds the 4 and −6, because the window sum stays below k, so it misses this.

hints: With prefix sums P, the subarray from i to j − 1 sums to P[j] − P[i]. For each end j, you want the latest start i with P[i] ≤ P[j] − k.
A plain two-pointer window fails because a negative number can make a longer window worth less. Which earlier prefix values can never be the best start?

Keep a deque of start indexes with increasing prefix sums. For each j, pop from the front while P[j] − P[front] ≥ k (record the length; that start will never give a shorter answer), then pop from the back while P[back] ≥ P[j], then push j.

explain.intuition:
Use prefix sums: P[0] = 0, P[j] = nums[0] + … + nums[j − 1]. A subarray is a pair of indexes i < j with sum P[j] − P[i]. For a fixed end j, a good start has a small prefix value and lies as far right as possible.

That rules out two kinds of starts. If a later index j has a prefix value no larger than an earlier one, the earlier start is dominated forever: the later one is both closer and at least as small. So keep start candidates in a deque with strictly increasing prefix values. And once a start at the front has produced an answer for some j, any later end would only make that subarray longer, so it can be dropped. Each index enters and leaves the deque once, which gives O(n).
steps: For j from 0 to n: while the deque is not empty and P[j] − P[front] ≥ k, update the best with j − front and pop the front.
While the deque is not empty and P[back] ≥ P[j], pop the back: j dominates it.
Return the best length, or -1 if none was found.
pitfalls: Using a two-pointer window that shrinks while the sum is at least k. Negative numbers break the monotonic sum it relies on.
Skipping the back pops and keeping every start in the deque. A larger prefix value then sits at the front, blocks the check, and the shorter answer behind it is never seen.
Using a heap of prefix sums. It finds a small prefix but not the latest one, and becomes O(n log n) at best.

solutions.title: Try every start
solutions.idea: For each start, extend to the right and stop at the first end where the running sum reaches k.

solutions.title: Monotonic deque over prefix sums
solutions.idea: Keep start indexes whose prefix sums increase. Pop the front when it already reaches k; pop the back when the new prefix is no larger.

followups: If every number were positive, what simpler technique would work, and why?
Find the longest subarray with sum at most k instead, still allowing negatives.
lcTitle: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
